posts.title: Leaving Home and Learning to Dream
posts.subtitle: Life Challenges, Finding Oneself, and the Deeper Meaning of Yaakov's Ladder — Rav Tzadok HaKohen's Kometz HaMinchah (II:70–72)
posts.author: Akiva Gutnicki
posts.excerpt: Why does Yaakov's journey begin in flight, stripped of everything, heading straight into the land of deceit? Drawing on Rav Tzadok HaKohen's Kometz HaMinchah (Sections 70–72), this essay explores leaving home, life challenges as ezer k'negdo, discovering the 'I' within, and the bigger idea of dreaming.
posts.dedication: Dedicated לְעִלּוּי נִשְׁמַת דְּבוֹרָה חַנָּה בַּת הָרַב נֹחַ (mother of Justin Eichel, on her third yahrtzeit) — may her neshamah have an aliyah.

blocks.text: 1. The Day Everything Changed: Leaving Home (בֶּן יוֹמוֹ)
״וַיֵּצֵא יַעֲקֹב מִבְּאֵר שָׁבַע וַיֵּלֶךְ חָרָנָה״

Parshas Vayeitzei opens with a quiet redundancy that every classical commentator notices: "Jacob departed from Beer-sheba, and he went to Haran." If the Torah already tells us he went to Haran, why pause to tell us that he departed from Beer-sheba?

In Kometz HaMinchah (Part II, Section 70)—a manuscript work where Rav Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin writes with striking poetic clarity about how to read the arc of a human life—he explains that those two verbs reflect two completely different reasons for the same journey. Leaving (וַיֵּצֵא) was Rivkah's command: purely an emergency flight (בְּרִיחָה) from a brother bent on murder, with no intention that Yaakov remain long enough to marry there. Going (וַיֵּלֶךְ) was Yitzchak's command: a purposeful mission to Charan to find his zivug and build a home. Rivkah never told Yitzchak about the threat; Yitzchak never knew his son was running for his life.

pairs.en: Yet the two were truly a single purpose.
This is the meaning of our Sages' statement: "On that very day."

pairs.he: רָצָה לוֹמַר, שֶׁהַיּוֹם גּוֹרֵם וּמְיֻחָד לְכָל מַעֲשֶׂה,
pairs.en: That is, the day contributes to each deed and is specially appointed for it.
Here, "on that very day" means that everything serves one purpose.

blocks.source: Rav Tzadok HaKohen, Kometz HaMinchah II:70

blocks.text: Most of us can look back at a pivotal ben yomo day in our own history—a day when we felt pushed out of somewhere comfortable, or when two seemingly unrelated turning points collided on the same afternoon. In the moment, leaving home feels like disruption or escape. Only later do we see that the day itself triggered a chain reaction of hashgachah, weaving what we were running from and what we were walking toward into one larger design meant to make us whole (שָׁלֵם).

Even more striking is when this departure happens. Yaakov has just received the blessings from his father—the spiritual peak of his youth. Rav Tzadok compares that moment to the Chassidic maxim, "Ein chozek k'chasidus b'techilaso"—there is no fervor like piety at its beginning. Yet immediately afterward, "Vayeitzei": he leaves home stripped of everything (עָרוֹם וְחָסֵר כֹּל), forced to surrender his possessions to Elifaz and grope forward in the dark. Leaving home is rarely a triumphal procession. Often, the moment right after our greatest inspiration is when the lights go out and the real journey begins.
2. Life Challenges as Your True Helper (עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ)

Where does providence send Yaakov—the quintessential "ish tam" (אִישׁ תָּם, a man of integrity), of whom Scripture declares "lo nachash b'Yaakov" (there is no divination in Jacob)? Straight into Aram—a name whose very letters spell ramai (רַמַּאי, deceit)—and among Bnei Kedem, a culture steeped in divination (נִחוּשִׁים).

Why couldn't Yaakov build his life in an environment that matched his nature? Here Rav Tzadok offers one of the most liberating reframings of human struggle in all of Chassidic thought. He defines the Torah's phrase ezer k'negdo (עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ)—"a helper opposite him"—in its starkest, most literal sense:
True help toward wholeness comes precisely from what stands opposite you. When a person becomes complete in that respect as well, his perfection is truly established.

Just as Avraham's ten tests ran directly counter to his natural attribute of boundless chesed, Yaakov's entire life—from the lentils and the blessings, through twenty years of Laban's trickery, his marriage to Leah (עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת, the mainstay of the household), the spotted rods, the confrontation with Esav, and even Yosef's elaborate setup with his brothers—was forged through encountering his exact opposite. Our natural strengths (מַעֲלוֹת) only reach so far; we cannot sharpen our blind spots (חֶסְרוֹנוֹת) by staying surrounded by people and situations that mirror our comfort zone. What opposes us, challenges us, and forces us to develop "ramaus b'makom shetzarich" (רַמָּאוּת בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁצָּרִיךְ)—strategic resilience where truth demands it—is not an interruption to our wholeness. It is the instrument of it.

Rav Tzadok pushes this insight even further, applying it to our personal failures: "V'chein Yisrael — hachataim hem ikar beirur shleimusam"—even Israel's sins are central to clarifying their perfection. The Hebrew word chet (חֵטְא) literally means chesaron (חִסָּרוֹן)—a lack, a missing piece. You might stumble once, twice, or a hundred times. Yet rather than merely condemning you, a struggle exposes the exact flaw corresponding to your personality that you are here to repair. Your hardest challenge becomes your ezer k'negdo—the very friction through which teshuvah transforms weakness into strength.

Still, the road from where we stand to where we need to be can feel impossibly long. Rav Tzadok quotes the Midrash: "The fool says, 'When will I ever learn all the Torah in the sage's heart?'"—and admits honestly, "Aruchah me'eretz midah" (its measure truly is longer than the earth). Left purely to ourselves, the distance is overwhelming. That is why Yaakov was granted kefitzas haderech (קְפִיצַת הַדֶּרֶךְ)—the miraculous shortening of the road. Beyond our spouse and beyond our struggles, there is a third partner to ezer k'negdo: the Holy One Himself (אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ), Who steps in with siyata d'Shmaya to bridge the distance our own effort cannot cross.
3. Finding Oneself in Exile: The House, the Stones, and the "I" Within

If Yaakov's destiny was to bring forth the twelve tribes of Israel, why did eleven of them have to be born outside the Land of Israel, in exile (גָּלוּת)? Rav Tzadok explains that in Eretz Yisrael—the realm of Yitzchak, who never left the Land—there is hakarah berurah, clear, direct awareness of God. And where everything is crystal clear, "ein sham yegiah v'avodah"—there is no real toil, no struggle, no freely chosen service. A complete nation—and a complete self—cannot be built in effortless daylight. It is built b'es harichuk (בְּעֵת הָרִחוּק), in the time of distance, when you have to choose who you are in the dark.

That is why Yaakov married both Rachel and Leah: to integrate the two concurrent worlds we inhabit every day—alma d'isgalya (עָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא, the revealed world of our visible daily deeds) and alma d'iskasya (עָלְמָא דְּאִתְכַּסְיָא, the concealed inner world where we wrestle with hidden providence). And it is why Yaakov's perfection is called mitah sheleimah (מִטָּה שְׁלֵמָה): not because he stayed sheltered inside his parents' home, but because "gam b'richuk makom lo zaz midibuko"—even in a distant land, he never let go of his attachment to Hashem. From Yaakov's journey was born the Talmudic promise: "B'chol makom shegalu, Shechinah imahem" (Megillah 29a). We associate the Shechinah with the Kotel or the Beis HaMikdash, yet its closest dwelling place is inside our own heart.

In Section 71 (אוֹת ע״א), Rav Tzadok shows how Yaakov discovers this inner sanctuary alone in the field: "Vayikach me'avnei hamakom"—"He took some of the stones of the place." Avraham had called the sacred site a Mountain (הַר), and Yitzchak had called it a Field (שָׂדֶה)—open terrains that anyone can wander into. Only Yaakov called it a House (בַּיִת, Beis Elokim): a bounded, secluded, tzanua space. He placed the stones around his head (וַיָּשֶׂם מְרַאֲשֹׁתָיו) because every action begins in the thoughts of the mind; guarding your inner headspace is how you lay the foundation stones of a home.

When those stones miraculously fused into one (מִתְאַחוֹת), the Midrash says Yaakov knew there was no dross (פְּסֹלֶת) left within him. Just as a house is built only when separate stones join into a single structure, finding oneself means bringing the fragmented pieces of life—Creator and created, past, present, and future—into the unity of Havayah (הָיָה, הֹוֶה, וְיִהְיֶה) and Shema Yisrael. And then Rav Tzadok delivers a sentence that turns the entire search for identity inside out:

pairs.en: For the Divine Presence is called "I":

pairs.he: רָצָה לוֹמַר: שֶׁהָאָדָם מְדַבֵּר ״אֲנִי״ וְרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
pairs.en: meaning that when a person says "I," he means Hashem, blessed be He,
for Hashem dwells literally within him—
"The Holy One in your midst," and the Divine Presence speaks through his throat.

blocks.source: Rav Tzadok HaKohen, Kometz HaMinchah II:71

blocks.text: When a parent's inner life reaches that hidden unity (יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה—bringing the Shechinah down "b'kerev ish v'lev amok," into the deepest chamber of the heart), it transmits naturally to the next generation—like the hidden Jewish children after the Holocaust who, upon hearing a rabbi recite Shema Yisrael, immediately cried out "Tatti" and "Mammi." To truly find oneself is not to inflate the ego; it is to quiet the noise until your deepest "I" becomes transparent to the Divine Presence living within you.
4. The Bigger Idea of Dreaming (וַיַּחֲלֹם and the Ladder of Sinai)
״וַיִּשְׁכַּב בַּמָּקוֹם הַהוּא וַיַּחֲלֹם וְהִנֵּה סֻלָּם מֻצָּב אַרְצָה״

We usually treat dreaming as passive—what happens when our conscious mind clocks out. Rav Tzadok reads vayachalom (וַיַּחֲלֹם) in the exact opposite way. Dreaming, he writes, is Yaakov's defining spiritual level (מַדְרֵגַת יַעֲקֹב): "He reaches a level at which further labor and struggle are no longer needed, and even lying down is good. This is the 'house,' where there is rest (מְנוּחָה)—whereas the mountain and field involve toil."

This is the level of Shabbat—the very root of Be'er Sheva ("the Well of Seven") that Yaakov carried inside him even after leaving home. When your waking choices, your boundaries, and your inner heart are truly aligned, you arrive at a place of inner rest where even your sleep, your dreams, your imagination, and the unguarded thoughts of your heart (בְּכָל דִּמְיוֹנוֹתָיו וְהִרְהוּרֵי לִבּוֹ) see only one reality: "V'hinei Hashem"—"And behold, Hashem." The bigger idea of dreaming is not escaping reality; it is integrating your soul so deeply that your subconscious itself becomes a sanctuary.

In Section 72 (אוֹת ע״ב), Rav Tzadok unpacks the ladder Yaakov sees in that dream as the complete map of human growth. The Sages teach "Sulam zeh Sinai" (סוּלָם זֶה סִינַי)—the ladder is Mount Sinai, spanning from the lowest member of Israel all the way up to Moshe Rabbeinu on the summit. Nobody starts at the top, and nobody is excluded from the climb. Crucially, the angels ascend and then descend (עֹלִים וְיֹרְדִים), "because a greater ascent is impossible without a descent." First you climb to a level, and then comes the fall. Yet right after the descent, the verse declares: "V'hinei Hashem nitzav alav"—"And behold, Hashem stands over him." Even at the bottom of a fall, Hashem has not walked away; recognizing His presence inside the descent is what lifts a person to a higher rung than they could ever have reached without falling.

Why was Sinai chosen over every towering peak? Because it was the lowest of mountains (Sotah 5a), embodying "Ani es daka" (אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא)—"I dwell with the contrite and lowly." By the analogy of "Hashem tzilecha" (ה׳ צִלְּךָ, "Hashem is your shadow"), when a person lowers himself in genuine humility—realizing he is nothing on his own—God, as it were, lowers Himself to meet him right where he stands. And at that moment, the Midrash says, the entire Land of Israel—the entire realm of spiritual clarity and grasp (מְקוֹם הַהַשָּׂגָה)—folds beneath his feet.
5. The Promise of Return (וְהִנֵּה אָנֹכִי עִמָּךְ)

At the end of the dream, Hashem seals Yaakov's journey with three great gifts—the Land ("lecha etnenah"), Israel ("v'hayah zar'acha"), and the Torah ("V'hinei Anokhi imach," echoing "Anokhi," the opening word of Sinai). When the awareness that "I am with you" stays constantly before your eyes—the opening principle of the Shulchan Aruch, "Shivisi Hashem l'negdi samid"—the entire Torah flows naturally from it.

And then comes the fourth promise, crowning the entire parashah: "V'hashivosicha... ki lo e'ezvecha"—"I will bring you back to this land, for I will not forsake you." Rav Tzadok explains that this promise is teshuvah—the spiritual level of King David and Mashiach ben David, who complete the four-legged chariot (מֶרְכָּבָה) alongside Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. No matter how abruptly you had to leave home, no matter how tangled the challenges of Aram become, no matter how far into the dark your descents take you—the promise "ki lo e'ezvecha" guarantees that no soul is ever permanently banished. Every departure carries within it the seed of return; every stone you rest your head upon in the dark can become the foundation of a house; and even in the middle of the night, the ladder is already standing right where you are.
